blocks.x: Adlib, you know, you can run a, if a man's got a number they're going to play a band or a hoist, and the important things is breaks, well you can adlib them things, then you go on your own, you understand, that's where the drum operation.
So it was when you were with that Navy band and you had to make it, you were playing with a Navy band, a big 18 piece, and you had to come down to this little 6 piece band.
Oh yeah, well that's in the field work, you understand, I would already play with them kind of bands, that's my kind of bands before I went in the Navy band.
Did you find yourself okay in that band?

Same, it's like, you didn't change from that same thing, you know, just want to have more men, you understand. Yeah, just more men, just like when I come out of the Navy band, the first, not a recording, but the first concert we played at the St. Charles Hotel was with Bunk Johnson and the George Lewis band, yeah. First night that you came in town, yeah, same trouble, baby, baby, baby, the doctor didn't come down, yeah. Oh. And they just come from making a tour in New York. I went to play, went to St. Charles Hotel. I didn't know that you had to play at the Bunk. Yeah, Bunk Johnson, sure, with George Lewis band, yeah, he, well. Well, we was lingering around here a while, and we were doing a little odd job, and trained folk these weekend jobs. Different outfits, you know. We were little weekend jobs, and we straggled, and then I went in, went in to work it, at the port of the government. I went out there with 16 bucks, played music, boss player. Now and then, I worked at the port, let's see. Then I believe in the year of 40, let's see, 49, on January 15, 49. I was waiting at the port then. I started the port, let's see, December, 47, December the 10th, something like that, 1947. Then that January, I mean December, that Christmas came in. I wasn't playing then. January, my mother died, 15th January, 1949. And I had a brother that lost him that same year in the month of May 22nd, same year, a few months ago, my mother. And then I worked all through that, still wasn't playing. Like I said, we used to work from Mondays to Fridays, night work seats for the government, 62 in the morning. And, uh, that's normally porting vacation. And then I came out of that, let's see, after six minutes, 16 months. Then they made a reduction in force, I'm thinking it comes to me now, 1950. Oh, yeah. The President Truman, the President of the United States, they made a reduction in all civil service employees, you see. And they showed us out in the field, let me see, when I saw the playing music again. Let me see what group I went with. I was spotting them, then, let me see, I went back to work for a place to call Leroy Johnson, who had been sent for me again. Yeah. Wait in the quartermaster department. And then Celestine, Robert Celestine was making up a band from the paddock, he's number two band. See, one section was playing with Bill Mackin on the paddock, and then he had another outfit he kept on to keep his outside work protected. Yeah. That band consisted of Louis Barbaran, Ray Pearson, Bretta Cohn, Bretta, and, uh, Mercedes on piano. And, uh, he was, he was using, uh, using all bass. Old man, uh, John Porter. John Porter, that's right, yeah. John Porter. And, uh, I called Louis Barbaran on drumming, Paul's brother. Yeah. The old man himself. Yeah. Then when the doctors made him get out to paddock, you see, that work was too hard for him, all that rush playing. Yeah. Then if he, uh, he wanted to put Louis out the band that he wanted me to, I went in the band 1951 or something like that, or 50, I think it was 1951. Oh, man. And I joined his band. And I played with him a good while. And he stopped using me, and he took Louis back in the band. He'd been with us ever since, you see.
Louis made a record with him, didn't he, with that, with that same band?
Yeah, his last band. And we did lots, I mean, I didn't make this last time I made the record, but we did a whole lot of, uh, television work for the, uh, we did a show around the town with Mr. Brown.
Uh-huh.
And then we did another television show at WDSU.
Oh, with Celestan.
Bob Celestan. Oh, man. Yeah, and we used to travel all out in Texas.
Why would Celestan like? He's a trumpet player, you know?
He's a good trumpet player. Yeah. Good trumpet man. Nice, soft, tonish. Good trumpet man.
Uh, so when did you go into Celestan?

Oh, yeah, I was playing, uh, let me see, then we, Me and Poison Humphrey, we were just working together. Them the fellas I forgot to mention. See, when we'd be living in the field, Me and Poison Humphrey, we'd be playing together like that, on and off, Em and all of us like that. And we decided to make that band strong, you know, just make, organize it like. Yeah. But Sweet Em and Esma, she used it. And the name first was titled from Miss Valente at the paddock. She's the one made Em use that adopted name of the bell girl.
Oh.

And Miss Valente gave her that idea. By playing and beating the rhythm with her two foots, she used to relief there on Tuesday nights. Yeah. Play relief nights in the... Oh, yeah. Well, you know, playing the piano is like a man playing a drum with an afterpeat like a stock house. Yeah. They gave her the ideas. And she put bells on her ankles.
And ankles.
Because Bill says, use the bells on your ankles. It's like a rhythm effect. Yeah. That's where that started from.
Yeah.

That time, with that band, was what Rick Howe was playing, Poison. And sometimes we had Piku with us. Yeah. Yeah. Mostly. Then we'd try to get Willie, but Willie was working with Paul Barber and sometimes with Fredrick Coleman, that. And the same block by Sid DeVille at Montegral. But we first started with Piku playing Clown and Poison. And we had a trombone player by the name of, he died not long ago. That man live uptown there. Not Piers? No, not late. What's his name?
Bob Thomas?
Bob Thomas. No, not Bobby.
I was a Dodge.
His name is a little, not French here. Joe Avery. Joe Avery, yeah. He played a good while with us. Joe Avery.
Mm-hmm.

And Emma and Rick Howe played. Yeah. Then when Piku stood there, then when Piku, I think Piku's out of getting feeling kind of bad. He used to alternate. He'd be with his wildest faces, you know. Sometimes we couldn't get Piku where we might use the answer and then we'd use the Andrew Morgan. Piku?
Piku.

Oh, Piku. Alphonse Piku, yeah. And we'd get Andrew Morgan or either we'd try to be getting that Willie, because Willie was working with Paul. That one, Willie, I don't know how you come out of Freddie's band, Freddie Coleman's band, my friend. Freddie got Sam Dutra to play Clown and well that showed Willie. He still was working with Paul and sometimes we could get him to come play with that. Yeah. Just that one night, you know. That's it. At the paddock with us, the relief band.
Why'd you come to go to that Cincinnati thing with Lawrence?

Well, that was, the people wanted Lawrence up there. They knew Lawrence from George Lewis' band. Oh, yeah. The Rosenthal's family. Yeah. His name is, he's crazy about George Lawrence. Yeah. George Rosenthal. People out in Cincinnati. Lawrence got the job, did he? Lawrence got the job and we made that Cincinnati trip.
What was that band called? Hmm? What was it called?
Well, it is, I know, I got the picture. You ever seen a picture of it?
Yeah, you showed me the picture.
Yeah, it was.
It was Lawrence Murray's band, was it?

Yeah, it was Lawrence Murray. He couldn't go on to George Lewis' title because it was an organized band. But George, George Rosenthal told him, let's get him a good city. But he know most of the men's coming up there because he was down here. He came down here when we even was working at the paddock. Then we made another group. We come out the paddock, we made another group. When George, one time George Lewis split his band. Some of these men that won't go on the road like, such as Jim Crow and Kid Howard, with George and Joe Waskin, with Joe the drummer. One day they went, they made a tour in Chicago, in Cincinnati. Well, during that time they was working at Mardi Gras Lounge. They said, the building. So Joe Waskin asked me to go play. They was going to leave on a Sunday for me to go in there and wait. The remainder of George Lewis' band, who was remaining was Kid Howard, Jim. So we got Emma to play piano and we had Willie to come in there a while on clarinet, take George Lewis' place. And we got on, we got on bass now. But I know George, Drag had left with George Lewis. I think Rick Howard, he came in on that deal too. I'm thinking it was Rick. No, Bro.
Well, uh, Bro. Well, uh, Bro.
MacNeil Bro. MacNeil Bro got Bro, that's right. Then we tried Ache on banjo. Oh, yeah. He had Ache in there a while. And Ache, he left and then we got George Guino.
Yes.

In the band here. That's working with Howard's outfit now. Oh, yeah. You see? Then that band stood near Goodwild. Then another time we took that group and went and worked just like Eminem at the paddock. The paddock will use a band where the first thing she stopped, that's what Miss Valencia did at the paddock. She might be in there a couple of weeks or a month. She'd get rid of that group and then try to mix the men's up with another group to play the release, you know. Then some fellas won't play in there. No. No.
Some people.

Yeah, plenty of musicians. You can't get them to play. They're ready to do without their money. I know lots of them. They won't play in the paddock. I know lots of them. And most old drummers, they're hard to get them to say it's too hard. That boy have trouble all doing it. It was a carnival season, trying to get off and get men to go in his place. Yeah. Bob Ozzie. Bob, yeah.
Fellas won't go. How did you come about playing drums?
Do you remember? Oh, I don't know. No, that's why I don't know when Bob started. I really don't know. You know his daddy's good. Yeah. You know when he plays daddy's the old drummer.
I was going to ask you, do you remember when Joe Walken came back into the Lewis band when you was out in the West Coast? Was it?
I put him back in the band. Yeah.
How did that come about?

Well, he was working out in San Francisco with a man called King Guglio and Earl Hans. And I guess they didn't like his style because how that all started, they was working, during that time, the whole band was working at the paddock. Which band?
George Lewis band.
George Lewis band. You see? And George had some bookings to go out to the West. George's band is famous on the West Coast.
George Lewis band.

All I can know is the West Coast. And he know the band already going to have a booking to go out there. But some fellas, you see, they get head swollen like that and they say they're not used to experience traveling. And when this, Earl Hans, that was a man who had what you call original. He was, we know he come from big bands out of Chicago. You would call them swing bands, you understand? That, I know that. Seen him and I heard him. And they form a band, a Dixieland group in San Francisco. And when they sent down here to get New Orleans jazz drumming, they do that sometimes. Mixing fellas. That's how they did Freda Coleman. They brought in foot with this big fine band in California. That big, I forget that. There's a white outfit. I forget them guys' names. But they just use him as a Dixieland man. Because he's good at drumming and playing with the big band. You could do that, but you see, a drummer can make a swing or a jazz. If you got a jazz drummer, you can take any, take five minutes out of the big band and you can make them play Dixieland style. I know I can do that with any big band. The way you play, you make them play that way. So, Freda did that, but he just had a month's work to do that. But Joe Watson went up with King Gurley and Earl Hans, them fellas. And then, that's why I understand why he wanted to quit. He's band at the paddock. He knew his band was going up there. You see? So, they all started warning me, ringing me at 2 o'clock in the morning. I was living on Arbor Street there. Well, Lawrence called me, my cousin. They asked me, George said, I said, sure, I play with George. I ain't doing nothing but the Spartan. So, he said, well, come at the paddock. They got two more weeks at the paddock before they go to California. Well, they said two weeks in a few days. Well, I went and started playing with Joe. He said, well, after Joe Watson left, because he had to ship off and go away to San Francisco. Well, I went to work for the men's to finish that job up. And then, we left here on a Sunday. And that Saturday night before we left, Lawrence suffered a stroke. Oh, yeah. You see? And that was it. And then, how we left that Sunday morning to go to San Francisco. We got to San Francisco that Tuesday at 1.30. We left here that Sunday morning, by railroad. And we played up there. And after we had, see, we had two weeks working in San Francisco, and three months, job in Los Angeles. But the Saturday morning we left San Francisco to come down to Los Angeles, every year in October they had what they called a Jazz Jubilee. Yeah. Big concert with bands all over the United States. Oh, yeah, that's Frank Gold. Yeah, that piece in the Coliseum and all bands take part in that. Yeah. Well, I met men up there. I ain't met in many years like Kid Ory, minor Hall and all them people. I ain't seen any musicians in years. Well, by being with George, when we left Frisco that morning, well, the same morning we was leaving France, San Francisco to come down to Los Angeles. It takes a train ten hours to run that. That's 481 miles by railroad. And we had to be at that. Well, we can make a train leave about eight something and get in Los Angeles, about six something in the evening. Concerts don't start until about 8 or 8.30 that night, you see. And then you got nine bands. Each band played half an hour. No. So we had plenty of time, you know. Then you'd have fellas that meet you with cabs and automobiles to bring you to the Coliseum or the tour. But I mean, that night, I mean that morning, that's where George told us that the fellas was kicking on Joe Watson. They don't like he can solo or something. I didn't worry about going to the Coliseum. We had nights off in San Francisco, but I didn't worry about going down there by the hangover where they was playing. I used to stay around the rooming house. And they wanted me to go. I said, I don't want to go. I don't feel like going. When I first got to Frisco, I was staying in the rooming house. So I got the man where we stopped. I knew them from here, the old man Jackson. They used to live on Burgundy in St. Peter. And people went up there during the wars and they accumulated a little money and they got their own rooming house, you see. And we used to sit down and talk. When we got there that Tuesday, we didn't have to go to work until that Friday, you see, of the same week and play that Friday Saturday. Then the next week we'd play a study from that Monday clean up to that Friday and then leave that Saturday and come to Los Angeles.
How come that Joe got back into the band and you left?

Then, yeah, when I came to Los Angeles, that's why George Lewis told us that they was, they put a, give him a two weeks notice, but I'd play, just pay in advance. That's the union laws. Yeah. So, Joe, King Goodall, try to help but, Earl Hines did that. So we left that morning and that's the same morning that happened to Joe Watkins, because he was living at the hangover club with George Lewis while we was in San Francisco. So when we go down to Los Angeles playing down there, he, well a few days after we was in Los Angeles, he came by there, you see. I mean a week after we was there and he came a few days after we played the first week and he was on his way home, you see. So I say whatever George put him back George didn't want with him mad since he quit the band now, you see. I say, well I'm going on back to New Orleans. New Orleans, but it's been like it is now. Like I had all my daughters out of Finn, but they didn't want me to go to all the people that liked it, because the first time I played in that place, I met.
took a life to my style of playing with Mr. Mr. The people on the...
Dr. Dolly?

All I know, the lady owns the play. My husband used to be an ex-policeman in California. But they all liked the way I... All the people, they heard me play, but the first time they see me in person. I never been to New York. But when I went to California, the people hear you, they might hear your names call, you see, but they never see you in person. They all liked the way I... So you just went back? I came on back. I bought Joe Waskin tickets, yeah. But the fellas didn't want me to do that. That part would give me, you know, fits for doing something like that. Because, you know, you're too good of a man, so you ought to sit up there and wait them three months out. But I had no trouble in that day. I just... I don't know. Let's go to this girl.
So who are you playing with right now, Sam?
Eminem, yeah, ever since I've been back here.
You recorded with it, didn't you, a little while back?

Yeah. But the people never could get over. Everybody, all of our family, people. I just didn't like Los Angeles. Me, but the job, it was a nice job. I mean, 125 hours a week on it. Couldn't beat that. 125 hours a week.
But what about us? 125. Sure.

George Gino was on there. That's why we had George Gino, because he met us a little before we left first, because of our Lord's suffering that stroke. But you see, if Joe Waskin wanted to come true then, you know, man, you get on the job saying, I know you can't leave a band like that, because that'd be wrong, because you can't pick up no Dixieland drummers and care not to fit them kind of, man. That's not an old-time band like that. And man, that'd be a real... Understand their style. You can run across good drummers, I know. That's it, yeah. But I know they wouldn't fit men like George Bush. It's like them fellas had their ideas of playing Earl Hines, you see. Now he might get a good, fast drummer, like, say, like Freddie one of them fellas, or maybe my playing, he might have kept fellas like me in these bands, you see. But you catch a fella like Earl. I know them fellas' style. They call themselves playing New Orleans style, but they're using them big bands, where they can turn the guy loose. For the man to tell you to take an eight-bar solo, you know, they trick you like this.
You ever work street parades on that? You ever worked some street parades on that?

All my life I worked street parades. I just started working street parades just the last few years. Now, then I hit him, man. I never cared. I got tired of it on the count of my knee worry, you see. I've been playing street parades all my life. Years and years. Brass bands, parades.
Played with Eureka on that?
Played with Eureka mostly. I played all Eureka's hard jobs. The last hard job the Eureka band played and they swore they wouldn't play. It was a jolly boy.
Oh, yeah.

Bill and him took part. I got the picture in there right now. Jolly boy, I don't know about that chair. That's the Sunday we lost. George Lewis fell out. He was working with John. I don't even know who the band he was. I think he was working with John. He was in Two Clown. I was with the Eureka band working at Alfred William's place. Alfred suffered with his heart and he couldn't make that level. It was a hot Sunday in August. Last Sunday in August. Temperature was 90. And hot sunny, snow clouds. Hot is scorching paving. Andres Rogers fell out. I'll tell you where he was. Red was the manager of the record, man. He fell out. All that started when we left Robinson and Orleans. See, we left this undertaker party here on Claiborne and...
That was his funeral, was it?

No, no. It was a record Jolly Boy parade. See, the Eastern Street, the other side, they call that Simon Boulevard. And we started walking through all the way up past the new railroad station. And the band not playing. You know, the band stopped playing. The minute we got to the canal and Basin Street, all that was beating Cadians on the snare, everybody walking. He wouldn't play. No, he wouldn't play. We didn't play all through that section. Just playing Cadians, people walking in the street. I beat Cadians on that snare drum from the... In fact, when we left Orleans and Robinson, we played a few numbers. And by the time we got to Bay Street, we cut out. Just started playing Cadians. I was with the record band. We had the lead first band. Poison didn't play that Sunday either. Poison laid off here. Poison wouldn't make them hard praise either. And Willie Pazio was on it. All the regular men and stuff. I think we had Kid Clayton in Poison's place. Oh, yeah. Yeah. And Willie Pazio had Sheets. All the regular men. Sonny Hendry had Alvin Warren and all the regular record band.
Yeah, I played the Tuxedo bands.

John.

He's an Alfred down there.

Yeah.

Alfred, no, I said, well, I said, relief him. That time I was waking the day, he called me to go pull him jobs for him. Well, that was the last Sunday I prayed. I believe that was around 50, I don't know if it was 52 or 55, something. But I know I wouldn't play no more because that was enough.
That was 52.
That was 52, but yeah. Because Doc's Sushi on the old and he gave me pictures of the parade. I keep it in a nice color, colorful to show. I like that. I keep that picture, yeah.

Yeah, how about the time beats that you use on the street, say the 6-8? You play the same sort of beats as you play in the 6-8 dance band things, like Gellysburg and whatnot. You play

Gellysburg and if you play the 6-8, you got that regular military beat, you know, that's the 6-8 two beats on the bass drum. You should play your syml even with the bass drum beats, because it looks, it's out of order to take the player, you're playing da-da-da-da-da-da, like that, it's more after beats, but you play the same beat with your bass and cymbals like a man doing, playing a regular military band. Gellysburg would you always play that in the 6-8? Funeral beats now for bass drum, you're supposed to give you, if you're beating a funeral kid, you're using a muffled drum, you see, and the trumpet player, he'll always give you a few little bars, make announcements, they're going to tell you what funeral they're going to pick up. you make a few beats, you'll be beating your regular, say, for example, the drummer is going dump, dump, dump, the counter player tells you, you know, you're walking regular cadenas, and you know the funeral monster and he might see, do that, you understand, you know the monster going to play, you just take your beats, you break your beats down, you go slow and all the time, he's down, down, down, down, down, down, you tell your bitch, he might holler to the bass drum player, watch me, see, that's what Mr. Pan used to do, snare drum, and he's down, down, all the time, he's gonna bring his down, down, and you see, you're just watching your men's, watch me, boom, boom, boom, boom, you understand, that's a real slow tempo, and the horns are big.
You
fall into your rolls, and then you can make, you ever see, some of these bands, they're so scary, man, you got your little pec band, and people making the same divisions, that's right, pec horn. You
don't just keep a roll like that one way.

Well, now that's where a man got the cup, he wanted to make that thing, he can make that same division them horns would make the same triplet, if he's got a good wrist, he can do it, or if not, he can stay in a roll. Oh, yeah.

Yeah. Still a sad man? Yeah, majority of the same men, yeah. Yeah. We made that band into the Young Tuxedo Band. And then we just add two more men stood. That's by adding a piano, a fella by the name of Dwight Newman.

Yeah, playing the piano. Yeah.

Yeah.
That's right, Lloyd Contrell, and a fella by the name of Don Albert.
Oh, yeah.

Yeah.

Yeah, but he was the title of Don Albert when he started traveling and all that. He made some records, didn't he, with Contra on. Yeah. Well, I don't know who he records, but I know he didn't record with us. Them days we didn't record, you know.
Well, he did something with Contra on.
Yeah, well, yeah, well, Contra was playing these bands.
Yeah.
Yeah, and when they had a big band down there, Contra played with him.

Oh, that's around in, let's see, it's 26, 25. It was, it ranged all around, say from 24 all through 26 like that. Oh, man. The old man was playing with P. Ron band. Mm-hmm.

Well, I used to talk, you live in the neighborhood, you see. I just passed, he was living right in the same block from my cousin Lawrence and them on the street they call in there, and that's Roman.
Oh, yeah.
And he was living on there, between Roman and Durban. Mm-hmm. And I passed there up and down all day long.
Yeah.
And we could see him, you know, and we'd talk, and he used to tell me, but he liked my style of playing and tried to get me interested in playing, tried to study drum notes. Mm-hmm.
Mm-hmm. Did you ever do that? You can read, can't you?
I read some drum chords, yeah. Mm-hmm. I hadn't played drum music in a good while since I flexed a bit out of the Navy band.
Mm-hmm. What did he teach you, you know, in, uh...
Willie Rudiman, did, then, uh, help with him, and then the first method, I, drum method I got was old Doc Lenny Bishy.
Oh, yeah.

Sidney's brother, yeah.

Yeah.

Yeah?

Yeah.

Oh, yeah.

Yeah.

Oh, yeah, Red Happy. Red Happy.
Black Happy. No, Red Happy. Yeah. No, not Black Happy.

segments.title: Drum ad-libbing and moving from Navy band to small bands
segments.summary: Frazier says a drummer ad-libs breaks; Allen asks about going from the big Navy band to small groups, which he says was his usual work.

segments.title: After the Navy: Bunk Johnson concert, port job and joining Celestin
segments.summary: Back from the Navy he plays the St. Charles Hotel with Bunk Johnson and George Lewis, works at the port, loses his mother and brother, is laid off in 1950, then joins Celestin's band replacing Louis Barbarin.

segments.title: Celestin band television work and travel
segments.summary: Frazier recalls TV shows and Texas travel with Celestin's last band; Celestin is called a good, soft-toned trumpeter.

segments.title: The Paddock relief band with Sweet Emma and Percy Humphrey
segments.summary: The relief band at the Paddock, how Sweet Emma got her bells, and the rotating cast of horn players.

segments.title: Cincinnati trip with Lawrence Murray's band
segments.summary: George Rosenthal's family wanted Lawrence in Cincinnati; Frazier explains the band's name and how Lewis's men were split up.

segments.title: Filling in at the Mardi Gras Lounge; how the Paddock mixed bands
segments.summary: Substituting for Lewis's men, trying banjoists, and the Paddock manager shuffling groups; many musicians refused to play there.

segments.title: Joining George Lewis for the West Coast after Joe Watkins leaves
segments.summary: Frazier replaces Joe Watkins, goes by train to San Francisco, plays the Jazz Jubilee in Los Angeles, and hears complaints about Watkins.

segments.title: Leaving Los Angeles and returning to New Orleans
segments.summary: He explains going home, Los Angeles audiences, and why Dixieland drummers do not suit an old-time band.

segments.title: Eureka Brass Band and the last parade he played
segments.summary: Frazier played street parades all his life, mostly with Eureka, and tells of the hot 1952 Jolly Boy parade where the band stopped playing.

segments.title: Ernest Trapanius's snare drum and Frazier's own drums
segments.summary: They discuss Alfred's duplex snare drum, once Trapanius's, and Frazier's plans to fix his drums with record money.

segments.title: The new records and wrapping up
segments.summary: Allen asks about the records Frazier made; he expects a hit and the interviewers ask if there is more.

segments.title: Beats for street parades, funerals and muffled drums
segments.summary: Frazier explains 6-8 military beats, funeral beats, signals from the trumpeter, and muffling a drum.

segments.title: First funeral after the Navy, playing bass drum
segments.summary: His first job after the Navy was a funeral in Algiers on bass drum with Peter Bocage and Paul Barbarin.

segments.title: Seating of drums and band on the street and in dance halls
segments.summary: Russell asks where bass and snare sit; Frazier describes the old dance hall seating order and advertising wagons.

segments.title: Wire brushes, hi-hat and low boy pedals
segments.summary: Frazier talks about wire brushes and his first hi-hat in the late 1930s.

segments.title: Family drummers, birth and first drum set
segments.summary: His brother Sam played drums; he was born 1904, taught himself, bought a snare around 1921 and a Conn set in the mid-1920s.

segments.title: The Golden Rule band and his Marrero cousins
segments.summary: His first band was a family group led by Bush Hall; he names cousins and uncle Bill's sons.

segments.title: Golden Rule becomes the Young Tuxedo Band
segments.summary: The band played local balls, became the Young Tuxedo Band, then spread into orchestras with Lloyd Cottrell and Don Albert.

segments.title: Lessons and influence from Cottrell and drum methods
segments.summary: Living near Cottrell he got pointers and encouragement to read, and a first method book from Doc Souchon's relation.

segments.title: Joining Piron's band in 1928 after Robichaux
segments.summary: Playing for Robichaux, he impressed Cottrell's circle and replaced Paul Barbarin when Barbarin left.

segments.title: Cottrell's style and Piron band's playing
segments.summary: Frazier describes Cottrell as a snare-roll timekeeper, mentions the Temple Roof Garden crowd, and whether he took solos.

segments.title: Piron's recordings and how drums were recorded
segments.summary: He recalls Piron's Victor recording and says that in early recording only cymbal and Chinese blocks were picked up.

segments.title: The Celestin Columbia record and Tuxedo band personnel
segments.summary: He lists musicians on the record, explains he was hired just for it, and describes early drum sets.

segments.title: The Idlewild riverboat job
segments.summary: After the Young Tuxedo Band, they played the Idlewild steamer in 1927.

segments.title: John Robichaux's band and radio work; Zutty Singleton and Red Happy
segments.summary: He lists the Robichaux band's men, its radio stock-music work, and drummers at the Lyric Theater.

segments.title: After Robichaux: Piron again and having no band of his own
segments.summary: He went back to Piron in 1928 and says he never led a band under his own name.

segments.title: The Navy dance band and ad-lib drumming
segments.summary: He compares the Navy band to outside bands, notes the men were rated musicians, and returns to ad-libbing breaks.
